S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by the presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both, that are time-consuming or cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges that the individual attempts to ignore or neutralize, while compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to these obsessions or according to rigid rules. The disorder often has a chronic course with waxing and waning severity, and may flare in response to stress, transitions, or health concerns. It is distinguished from psychotic disorders by the individual’s recognition that the thoughts and behaviors are excessive or unreasonable, and from generalized anxiety by the presence of specific intrusive cognitions and ritualized responses.

patient.stressor: In her late seventies, after a minor stroke and the death of a close sister back in India, Anantha became acutely aware of her own aging and vulnerability, especially while living alone in her suburban Illinois home. Her long-standing tendency toward meticulous bookkeeping and careful planning gradually shifted into an increasingly rigid preoccupation with whether she had overlooked something that might endanger her health or finances, particularly when managing medications and medical appointments. This intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, when isolation, constant health warnings, and reduced in-person contact with her mentees and community groups left her with fewer distractions and more time to dwell on worst-case scenarios about getting sick or making a catastrophic mistake. The condition became clinically significant when her worries about making an error with her medications and important documents began to delay her from leaving the house for community events and even medical visits, prompting her primary care physician, who noticed missed appointments and escalating distress, to refer her for psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “My mind keeps getting stuck on ‘what if I missed something important and it harms me or my family,’ and I can’t seem to turn those thoughts off.”

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: All day my mind keeps circling back to thoughts like, ‘What if I mixed up my morning and evening pills and have a stroke in my sleep, and no one knows,’ or ‘What if I misread a letter from the bank and lose the house for the children,’ and even when I tell myself it’s unreasonable, the fear that I’ve overlooked some tiny but disastrous detail just won’t let go of me.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: Because of these worries, I find myself rereading my medication list and appointment cards over and over, checking the pill organizer and the calendar three, four, sometimes five times before I can leave the house or go to bed, and even then I often go back one more time “just to be sure,” which makes me late or keeps me up much longer than I intend.
